When Anna Gordon sang the ballad of "Tam Lin" for a collector in 1783, and again for a different collector eighteen years later, the two texts did not match. Lines had moved; a stanza present in the first was absent in the second; a rhyme had been repaired. The collectors, who wanted the ballad, treated the difference as damage — the memory of an old woman failing under the weight of a long poem.

Later work has made that reading hard to keep. Singers in living ballad traditions have been recorded three and four times over a decade, and the pattern of their variation is not random decay. Formulaic phrases are exchanged for other formulaic phrases of the same shape. Whole scenes survive intact while the connective lines between them are rebuilt. Singers shown the two transcripts side by side are often unbothered, and say they sang it right both times.

The difficulty this creates for a collector is practical rather than philosophical. A printed page holds one version. Whichever performance is written down becomes, for every reader afterwards, the ballad; the others become variants of it, and the direction of that relation is decided by the accident of which night the collector was present. Some editors responded by printing several texts side by side, which preserves the evidence and abandons any claim to a single work. Others assembled a composite from the best lines of each, producing a poem that no one had ever sung.

Neither solution is wrong so much as incomplete, because both are answers to a question the tradition does not ask. Anna Gordon was not producing a text. She was doing something closer to what a musician does with a tune that is known to everyone in the room. The score is a record of one performance; the tradition is the capacity to give another.
